documents.abstract: La reseña analiza Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine), destacando su aportación al estudio de las transformaciones del trabajo derivadas de la inteligencia artificial. Se valora especialmente su concepción de la IA como una tecnología de propósito general y la introducción del concepto de expertise translacional como eje para comprender la evolución de las competencias humanas en los entornos laborales. Al mismo tiempo, la reseña señala algunas limitaciones de la obra, entre ellas la escasa atención prestada a la salud laboral, los riesgos psicosociales y las desigualdades estructurales que condicionan la incorporación de la IA en distintos contextos nacionales. En conjunto, concluye que el informe constituye una referencia de gran relevancia por su solidez analítica y por su capacidad para estimular nuevas líneas de investigación sobre trabajo, tecnología e instituciones.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Institutional representations condense heterogeneous histories into classifications, records, and indicators that may shape consequential decisions. This paper asks when an institution can responsibly rely on a reduced description while retaining the capacity to recognize, examine, and respond to challenges that its own categories may obscure. The central thesis is conditional: representational adequacy for a declared question, evidential access, review competence, effective correction, and the legitimacy of the governing criteria require distinct warrants. None alone establishes the others. Elementary results on factorization, approximation, indistinguishability, and guarded reachability identify where particular inferences fail under stipulated assumptions; they establish neither moral verdicts nor institutional powers. Renormalization supplies a bounded analogy rather than a demonstrated physical scaling law for institutions. Drawing on work in classification, epistemic injustice, sociotechnical abstraction, and accountability, the paper proposes a question-indexed, seven-part cross-stage inquiry covering recognition, evidence, access, competence, transfer, response, and frame review. Its incremental value lies in locating the precise stage and missing warrant between an identifiable representational distinction and a potentially consequential institutional response, rather than introducing new mathematics or generic audit principles. Fourteen propositions are editorially classified by mathematical role and inferential limits. Constructed cases consider excluded claims, feedback, protected evidence, referrals, competing remedies, and challenges to evaluative rules. A prospective protocol compares the proposed integrated register with competent existing procedures, including the possibility of equivalent performance, greater burden, unsafe disclosure, and inconclusive effects. No empirical implementation, legal validation, causal estimate, or independent moral proof is claimed. The result is a bounded investigative method whose usefulness depends on independently warranted questions, reliable evidence, legitimate institutional authority, and comparative performance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose Novelty is commonly regarded as one component of high-quality scholarship. Nevertheless, little is known about how novelty is claimed and what is considered novel across academia, including any field differences. In response, this article uses a sequential design to investigate novelty claims and field differences in academic research. Design/methodology/approach First, a simple classification scheme was created for theory, methods, data, integrative synthesis and contextual transfer novelties. Next, the Large Language Models (LLMs) Gemma 3 27B, GPT-OSS-120B and GPT-OSS-20B were used to identify original contributions in articles from the full texts of eight large journals representing contrasting general fields. Finally, a random sample of 50 articles per journal was classified by the authors with the same scheme and the results compared. Findings The three LLMs tested achieved moderate or substantial agreement with academic coders on the occurrence of data, theory and methods novelty within full text journal articles, but there was little agreement within and between humans and LLMs on integrative synthesis and contextual transfer novelties, suggesting that they may not be well defined concepts. There were also substantial field differences in the prevalence of data, theory and methods novelty. Practical implications Authors and reviewers should be careful to identify valid research contributions in interdisciplinary research or fields other than their home fields. Originality/value This is the first attempt to automatically classify academic research theory types.

Background: Artificial intelligence is increasingly influencing healthcare delivery and nursing education. Understanding nursing students' perceptions is important for preparing future professionals to use AI responsibly. Objective: To assess nursing students' awareness, experiences, perceptions, and training needs concerning artificial intelligence in healthcare. Methods: A descriptive, survey-based study was conducted among 175 nursing students at Cihan University-Erbil, Iraq. Data were collected using a 22-item closed-ended questionnaire and summarized using descriptive statistics. Results: Most participants were aware of AI (81.7%), and 56.6% reported previous AI use. Approximately 64.6% believed that deep learning-based AI could improve patient care, while 68.0% recognized its potential to facilitate communication across language barriers. Only 30.3% had received formal AI training, and 63.4% believed that additional training was necessary. Concerns included possible reductions in human nursing skills through excessive AI dependence. Conclusion: Nursing students demonstrated substantial awareness of AI and generally positive perceptions of its potential applications. However, limited formal training and concerns about professional skills indicate the need for structured AI education, ethical guidance, and continued human oversight. Further research involving multiple institutions is recommended.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), most pointedly through advancements in large language models (LLMs), has dominated the media and has expansive promise in improving productivity in a myriad of fields, notably the life sciences. The expansion of AI into the field has encompassed nearly every domain from research to healthcare and appears to have an inertia that will make it difficult to change the course of its adoption. Given this rapid pace of adoption, it is crucial to reflect on these advancements and their place in the modern life sciences to understand the evolving ethical, medico-legal, and scientific challenges the use of such technology poses for practitioners of the life sciences, specifically, the biomedical sciences. Herein, the authors narratively review the current usage of AI with respect to clinical care, research production and integrity, as well as an epidemiologic purview of technology.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Organizational behaviour explains how people interpret, experience, and influence work in conditions shaped by relationships, institutions, technologies, and unequal authority. This chapter develops a multilevel, critically grounded account of workplace psychology that connects individual motivation and cognition to teams, communication, power, conflict, culture, wellbeing, and algorithmic management. Its method is a transparent, purposive synthesis of foundational theory, peer-reviewed research, methodological literature, international guidance, and official Rwandan secondary data available by 24 October 2026. Competing explanations are tested against practical managerial decisions rather than presented as interchangeable prescriptions. An original multilevel behaviour-to-performance model, motivation comparison matrix, communication diagnostic, and negotiation simulation provide tools for professional inquiry. Rwanda's 2024 business-enterprise evidence and August 2026 labour-force statistics establish important contextual boundaries without being misrepresented as employee-attitude surveys. A fully hypothetical hybrid Kigali service enterprise illustrates work overload, information failure, psychological safety, measurement bias, and a phased intervention evaluated through transparent calculations. International comparison draws on a randomized hybrid-work experiment in China while examining differences in occupational composition, digital access, supervision, and economic vulnerability. The central thesis is that workplace behaviour is neither simply an individual trait nor an outcome fully controllable by management. It is a contingent result of psychological processes interacting with work arrangements, group norms, institutional power, and resource constraints. Ethical enterprise practice requires interventions that are empirically contestable, proportionate, intelligible to workers, and subject to independent correction.

Organizational structure determines how work, authority, information, accountability, and interdependence are arranged; organizational design determines whether those arrangements remain appropriate as enterprise commitments and conditions change. This chapter develops a critical, integrative treatment of structure and organizational change across firms, cooperatives, public institutions, and digitally mediated networks. It compares contingency theory, information-processing approaches, sociotechnical systems, organizational ecology, institutional theory, and organizational ambidexterity, identifying their explanatory mechanisms, competing predictions, and empirical limitations. The analysis develops twelve connected domains, from specialization, structural configurations, coordination, culture, and growth to diagnostic methods, change programmes, distributed work, innovation, and design justice. A transparent secondary-source synthesis draws on original scholarship, Rwanda's Integrated Business Enterprise Survey 2024, East African Community institutional arrangements, and peer-reviewed international hybrid-work evidence. Original decision-support instruments include a structure-selection decision tree, a structural trade-off matrix, a cross-functional workflow diagnostic, a governance and escalation design, and reproducible redesign economics. A hypothetical Kigali service enterprise and a documented regional institution demonstrate why formal reporting lines are insufficient without decision rights, resources, credible information, and equitable working practices. The chapter argues that effective structure is a provisional, revisable arrangement for handling essential interdependencies at acceptable coordination, human, and legitimacy costs. This proposition is conceptual, not a claim of newly established causal effects.

Computer-using agents are increasingly capable of performing complex tasks in the digital world. However, high-quality interaction trajectories remain scarce for specialized desktop applications, where limited application knowledge, cumbersome GUI workflows, and incomplete exploration hinder automated collection. We introduce OS-Wizard, an automated trajectory collection framework. It combines tutorial-guided exploration with a hybrid GUI--Code action space, providing application-specific knowledge and simplifying GUI workflows through direct execution of application-native commands. The framework also checkpoints and revisits pivotal states during tree exploration to explore alternative workflows, complementing linear rollouts for broader coverage. We collect 10.9K trajectories comprising 54.9K state--action samples. Fine-tuning open-source base models on this corpus yields a best-performing model that improves performance on a benchmark of specialized desktop workflows by 58.2 percentage points to 64.1\%, surpassing reported human performance of 59.8\% and establishing a new state of the art. The fine-tuned model also improves performance on general desktop workflows using GUI actions only, suggesting that the collected supervision benefits general desktop tasks as well. Comparative experiments and ablations demonstrate the efficiency of trajectory collection and the importance of code actions.

The transformation of Indonesian for Foreign Speakers (BIPA) learning is increasingly characterized by online platforms, interactive media, and artificial intelligence, while empirical evidence on their pedagogical functions, learning outcomes, and limitations remains dispersed across heterogeneous research designs. This study maps the forms of digital technology and artificial intelligence use, targeted language skills or competencies, reported benefits, and implementation challenges in BIPA learning. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted using the PRISMA 2020 flow for publications from 2022 to 2026. Indonesian sources were restricted to SINTA 2 and SINTA 3 journals, whereas international sources were used selectively when national evidence on artificial intelligence was insufficient and full open-access texts were available. The structured search log contained 26 unique records with initial relevance; 17 articles underwent full-text assessment and 14 empirical studies met the criteria for the primary synthesis. The findings reveal four dominant technology groups: web-based platforms and virtual learning environments, video or audiovisual media, interactive and gamified media, and artificial intelligence. Digital technologies mainly expand access, flexibility, interaction, cultural understanding, and opportunities to develop reading, speaking, and writing skills. Evidence on artificial intelligence remains more limited, although AI-based text-to-speech demonstrates strong potential for pronunciation training, while AI and augmented reality integration supports culturally oriented digital materials. Reported constraints include internet connectivity, limited generalizability, feedback accuracy, voice naturalness, cultural context, technology dependence, and data privacy. Digital technology and artificial intelligence are therefore best positioned as pedagogical supports that remain mediated by BIPA teachers.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare has accelerated globally, with increasing numbers of patients using AI-mediated platforms for medication consultation. This study aims to explore the views of pharmacists on this practice, providing evidence for the integration of AI into pharmaceutical services. A qualitative study was conducted via semi-structured face-to-face interviews with 10 pharmacists from Zhongshan Hospital of Xiamen University in Fujian Province, China. Purposive sampling was employed to include pharmacists with diverse professional backgrounds and experience. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and data were analyzed using thematic analysis with NVivo 15. Seven core themes were identified. Pharmacists generally favored patients using AI for medication information, acknowledging its merits and recognized its value as an auxiliary tool for health education and efficiency improvement, while highlighting its limitations in complex clinical scenarios and information reliability. Patient-related factors also affected the application of AI. Pharmacists emphasized their irreplaceable advantages in personalized guidance, humanistic care, and risk identification, and noted that AI popularization may reshape consultation volumes, communication dynamics, and professional competence requirements for pharmacists, alongside proposing targeted usage recommendations. This study explored the perceptions of pharmacists on AI-mediated medication consultation, highlighting the auxiliary potential of AI and the irreplaceable role of pharmacists. The findings provide a basis for policy formulation, AI application training, and AI optimization to promote rational integration and medication safety.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative AI and agentic tools are reshaping agile software development, yet many engineering curricula still teach agile methods and AI competencies separately and largely lecture-based. This paper presents a project-based AI Engineering curriculum designed to prepare students for AI-driven agile development by integrating agile practices and AI-enabled engineering throughout the program. We contribute (1) the curriculum concept and guiding principles, (2) a case study of interdisciplinary, AI-enabled agile student projects, and (3) early evidence from a mixed-methods evaluation. In our case study, second-semester bachelor students work in teams over seven two-week sprints on a realistic software product. AI tools are embedded into everyday agile engineering tasks—requirements clarification, backlog refinement, architectural reasoning, coding support, testing, and documentation—paired with reflection on human responsibility and quality. Initial results indicate that the integrated approach supports hands-on competence development in AI-assisted engineering. Key observations highlight the need for agile teaching adaptations due to rapid tool evolution, the critical role of oral verification to ensure foundational learning. We close with lessons learned and recommendations for educators designing agile project-based curricula in the age of AI.

Narrow-band imaging (NBI) enhances mucosal and vascular contrast and has become an important modality for the early detection of laryngeal cancer. Although radiomics enables the extraction of high-dimensional quantitative features from NBI images for computer-assisted diagnosis, the limited availability and heterogeneity of annotated datasets constrain the development and generalizability of machine-learning models. We propose a novel generative AI framework that improves radiomics-based classification. Instead of generating synthetic medical images, the proposed framework trains generative models directly in the radiomic feature space to learn realistic feature distributions and generate valid synthetic radiomic representations. The framework was evaluated with multiple machine-learning classifiers on a laryngeal cancer diagnosis task using a dataset comprising 11,144 NBI images from 210 adult patients, including 180 patients in the development set and 30 patients in an independent internal held-out test set. Performance was evaluated on an independent unseen test set using , accuracy, precision recall and F1-score. Generative augmentation consistently improved classification performance across all evaluated classifiers. Among the evaluated generative models, Generative Adversarial Networks achieved the most consistent improvements. Radiomics-GAN yielded the highest Median value of F1-scores of 0.851, outperforming the SMOTE-balanced baseline model without GenAI (F1-score: 0.806) on the test set. By enriching the radiomic feature manifold without generating synthetic medical images, the proposed framework effectively mitigates sample scarcity, improves classifier performance, and supports the development of more robust AI-assisted tools for laryngeal cancer diagnosis. Future work will focus on external validation and conditional generative models tailored to lesion subtypes and imaging acquisition variability.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT As the second most widely used metallic material after steel, research on the corrosion resistance of aluminum (Al) alloys holds great significance. To overcome the inherent limitations of experimental methods in capturing long‐term multifactor corrosion behavior of Al alloys, this review summarizes recent advancements in the multiscale simulation of their corrosion behavior. Although previous reviews have addressed individual simulation techniques or specific corrosion phenomena, a framework linking model capability, scale transfer, alloy characteristics, and engineering applicability remains limited. This review provides a systematic comparison of representative coupled multiscale frameworks in terms of their applicable scales, input parameters, output capabilities, advantages, and limitations. First, an overview of various Al alloy series is provided, highlighting their specific material characteristics and corrosion failure modes. Subsequently, simulation methodologies across distinct scales, ranging from the atomic level for unveiling corrosion thermodynamics and kinetics, to mesoscopic and macroscopic scales for predicting morphological evolution and performance degradation, are summarized. After that, multiphysics and multiscale simulation strategies, focusing on data transfer methods between different scales, are explored. Specifically, detailed descriptions of density functional theory (DFT)‐molecular dynamics (MD), MD‐phase field (PF), finite element method (FEM)‐machine learning (ML), and DFT‐MD‐ML coupled models are provided. Finally, engineering applications and future prospects are discussed, emphasizing the necessity of overcoming challenges in data transfer and highlighting the potential of artificial intelligence in achieving intelligent corrosion management.

Abstract Agile teams need fast, actionable feedback to manage Technical Debt (TD). However, refactoring is often postponed due to time pressure. Generative AI (GenAI) promises to accelerate refactoring, but its effect on maintainability, TD at the source code level, and code correctness is still unclear. We conducted a case study in a team-based agile course, where 46 student teams refactored Kotlin code using either GPT (23 teams) or Gemini in Android Studio (23 teams). Each team selected two files and applied iterative GenAI-assisted refactoring. We analyzed a total of 19,404 lines of code. We assessed changes using SonarQube metrics (code smells, TD estimates, complexity, and size metrics). We also analyzed responses from a post-activity survey on perceived usefulness and trust. GenAI-assisted refactoring reduced total code smells, SonarQube-estimated TD, and cognitive complexity, while total cyclomatic complexity increased, although average cyclomatic complexity per function decreased markedly.

Abstract China’s existing employee pension insurance system is designed for traditional stable employment, which cannot well adapt to labor dispatch, daily‑wage jobs and other fragmented flexible‑employment scenarios. With roughly 200 million flexible employees nationwide and a low pension‑insurance participation rate, prominent problems include employers’ evasion of social‑insurance contributions, fragmented contribution records and impaired contributory rights of gig workers. This paper proposes a reform framework of “dual‑account parallel operation, daily accumulation and unified settlement at retirement”. The reform retains the traditional pooled pension account (Account A) for formal full‑time employees and creates a new daily‑accumulation personal account (Account B) for flexible workers. Account B takes the natural day as the minimum contribution unit; both employer and employee contributions are credited to an individual closed‑end account rather than entering the social pooling fund. Upon reaching the statutory retirement age, participants may choose one of three settlement schemes: consolidated lifelong pension receipt, partial fund withdrawal, or full cash‑out of eligible accounts. Relying on tax‑authority fund‑flow supervision, the system aims to curb contribution evasion and safeguard workers’ contributory rights without undermining the fiscal sustainability of the existing pooling system. Nevertheless, this proposal still has practical constraints. The fully‑funded Account B lacks built‑in social solidarity; early lump‑sum withdrawal may trigger myopic consumption and potential old‑age‑poverty risks. Implementation will bring higher administrative workload, and grey‑market cash‑based labor payments cannot be completely eliminated. Further actuarial calibration of parameters such as withdrawal thresholds is required. This scheme provides a feasible policy reference for improving social security for new‑form labor groups. AI‑Assisted Statement This paper uses artificial‑intelligence tools for text organization, logical polishing and English‑language drafting. All core institutional design, research ideas and analytical viewpoints are independently conceived by the author. Relevant content has been revised and reviewed by the author.

Deepfakes reveal a gap between harm that is obvious to the senses and blame that can be attributed. Stating the law as on 13 October 2026, this article analyses India’s Information Technology Act, 2000 and the amended intermediary rules, along with the relevant constitutional and personality-rights case law. By way of doctrinal analysis, it distinguishes the elements of offences from regulatory obligations to prevent harm, from the conditions of intermediary exemption and from civil remedies. The amendments of February 2026 establish synthetic-content labelling, provenance requirements and differentiated takedown deadlines, yet do not turn every failure to comply into criminal liability. While existing laws cover a number of the fraudulent impersonation and sexual exploitation elements inherent in these cases, wholly synthetic intimate imagery, the evidentiary attribution of content to a particular person and parallel access to remedies remain difficult. The analysis therefore proceeds on a differentiated account of responsibility, in which the conduct, knowledge, control and available immunity of each participant are addressed separately once an underlying wrong has been identified. It advocates clear, tailored guidance, proportionate verification and victim-centred processes, as opposed to blanket developer liability. Regulation is effective only with responsible attribution, not merely with the rapid removal of content or the disclosure of synthetic origin.

Purpose This study reinterprets S. R. Ranganathan’s Five Laws of Library Science within contemporary artificial intelligence (AI)-driven library environments and explores how artificial intelligence is reshaping the philosophical, ethical, and institutional foundations of libraries. The study further examines how national libraries may increasingly function as human-centered public knowledge infrastructures within emerging AI-mediated information societies. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a conceptual and interpretive approach combining theoretical analysis, critical literature review, and institutionally situated discussion. Drawing upon scholarship concerning library philosophy, artificial intelligence, human-centered AI, semantic knowledge systems, and AI governance, the study develops a conceptual framework for interpreting AI-driven transformation through the philosophical lens of Ranganathan’s Five Laws. The National Library of Korea is discussed as an illustrative institutional context through which contemporary AI-related developments in national libraries may be interpreted. Findings The analysis suggests that artificial intelligence significantly expands and recontextualizes the philosophical assumptions embedded within Ranganathan’s Five Laws. AI-driven library environments increasingly transform traditional understandings of accessibility, discoverability, personalization, efficiency, and institutional growth through semantic retrieval systems, conversational AI, intelligent metadata infrastructures, and multimodal knowledge services. At the same time, AI-mediated library transformation introduces important ethical and institutional tensions involving algorithmic bias, misinformation, privacy, transparency, intellectual freedom, and public trust. The study argues that the continuing relevance of Ranganathan’s philosophy lies in its adaptability as a human-centered normative framework for guiding libraries within intelligent information societies. Originality/value This study contributes to contemporary library and information science scholarship by conceptually connecting classical library philosophy with emerging discussions concerning human-centered AI, trustworthy knowledge ecosystems, AI governance, and the evolving role of national libraries. While recent work has also explicitly connected Ranganathan’s Five Laws with artificial intelligence (Kalbande, 2025), this study differentiates its contribution by examining national libraries as public knowledge infrastructures and by linking each law to documented institutional illustrations and cross-cutting ethical conditions. The study therefore frames AI-driven library transformation as a broader philosophical and institutional shift affecting the public role of national libraries.
keywords: Ranganathan's Five Laws of Library Science

documents.abstract: Aim and objectives: To examine the diagnostic scope, accuracy and limitations of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based remote orthodontic monitoring for automated triage and to assess whether such systems can safely decide when orthodontic patients need in-person care. Methods: Narrative review of PubMed literature on AI-driven remote monitoring and tele-orthodontics, focusing on diagnostic performance, triage applications and the limitations relevant to distinguishing routine virtual review from urgent in-person care. Results: AI reliably detects visually obvious conditions with high specificity, but sensitivity is variable and often low for periodontal changes and precise tooth-level tracking. GO/NO-GO outputs can be inconsistent, radiographic complications such as root resorption cannot be assessed from photographs and single-center models lose accuracy when applied elsewhere. Early triage trials show faster screening yet still require clinician review for borderline cases. Conclusion: Current evidence indicates that AI is not yet safely autonomous for orthodontic triage. Clinician oversight, standardized triage thresholds, external validation and clear medico-legal frameworks remain essential.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Research and Teaching on AI and Leadership This teaching document presents a 14-week graduate seminar that examines artificial intelligence through the lens of higher education leadership. Students evaluate AI research, institutional policies, governance structures, academic integrity, privacy, accessibility, and leadership responsibilities while developing case studies and research proposals. The resource is designed for graduate students, doctoral candidates, and faculty interested in AI-related institutional decision-making.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyze the resilience of the Indonesian Navy's Command and Control (C2) in facing communication and information disruptions during maritime operations through a systematic literature review. The method employed was a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to identify, analyze, and synthesize findings from relevant studies. The results identify a complex spectrum of communication and information threats, including cyberattacks on Operational Technology (OT) infrastructure and Integrated Navigation Systems (INS), Denial of Service (DoS) attacks, GNSS spoofing, and system vulnerability exploitation, all of which can compromise C2 functions. These disruptions significantly degrade situational awareness (SA) and impede decision-making, potentially leading to mission failures or unintended escalation. Resilience-enhancing mechanisms include comprehensive cybersecurity implementation, the use of blockchain technology and hybrid cryptography, AI/ML for anomaly detection, and the development of integrated communication architectures based on SDN/SDR. Communication system redundancy through diverse channels is a primary strategy, supported by anti-jamming technology and strong encryption. This study extends operational resilience theory by positing the convergence of cybersecurity technologies and adaptive architectures as complementary mechanisms within the context of military maritime operations. The research implications provide a foundation for the Indonesian Navy to design a comprehensive C2 resilience framework that integrates advanced technical solutions with adaptive operational doctrine, enhancing sustained operational capabilities amidst evolving cyber threats.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into criminal justice has created opportunities to support crime analysis, investigative processes, legal research, and risk assessment. However, the use of AI in decisions affecting liberty and fundamental rights raises important ethical concerns. This paper examines four interconnected challenges associated with AI-driven decision-making in criminal justice: algorithmic bias, limited transparency, accountability gaps, and potential violations of privacy and human rights. Drawing on the themes developed in the underlying thesis and its reviewed literature, the paper develops a conceptual ethical framework for the responsible deployment of AI in criminal justice. The proposed framework emphasizes representative data, explainable decision-making, independent auditing, clearly assigned institutional responsibility, meaningful human oversight, and accessible mechanisms for contesting adverse decisions. It also considers the risks of predictive policing, surveillance technologies, and automated risk assessment. The paper argues that technical performance alone is insufficient to establish the legitimacy of AI-assisted criminal justice decisions. Responsible deployment requires continuous evaluation of fairness, protection of individual rights, and effective legal and institutional safeguards. The framework is intended to support researchers, policymakers, technology developers, and criminal justice institutions in assessing the ethical acceptability of AI systems
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes strategic decisions that determine how organisations allocate resources, restructure work and treat the people affected by those choices. Yet research has examined the performance benefits and the governance risks of AI largely in isolation, leaving the sustainability implications of delegated algorithmic authority under-theorised. Following PRISMA 2020, this study synthesises 50 studies, identified through four database searches covering 2019–2025 and backward citation tracking, using inductive thematic analysis. Six themes emerge: AI-driven automation and decision support, data-driven strategic decision-making, ethical and governance challenges, data security and privacy, organisational and structural impact, and innovation and competitive advantage. Together, these themes show that performance and governance concerns receive comparable attention (28 and 27 studies) but are rarely addressed together: only five studies span both. Building on these connections, the study develops a governance framework for socially sustainable, AI-enabled strategy. The framework conceptualises responsible AI as a socio-technical capability built on transparency, human–AI complementarity and organisational readiness, and calibrates the degree of algorithmic authority to decision criticality and EU AI Act obligations. The main contribution is therefore an integrative framework that keeps AI-supported strategic decisions both effective and accountable to those they affect, with implications for SDGs 8 and 16.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This discussion paper reconsiders the possible formation, persistence, migration, and partial dissolution of monetary mediation within evolving relations of production and exchange. Its starting point is the heterogeneous need for others: access to persons and communities, productive capacities, labour, knowledge, relations, and outputs can motivate exchange while leaving the institutional formation of monetary claims contingent. The analysis distinguishes needs, value circulation, monetary obligations, payment instruments, and the continued reproduction of productive conditions. It examines the conditional transformation of human–human, human–AI, and AI–AI monetary relations as artificial intelligence increasingly participates in production. A principal hypothesis is that monetary reliance may diminish locally through direct provision, multilateral commitments, admissible cyclic clearing, and institutionally supported coordination, while remaining present or re-emerging elsewhere. The proposed spacetime-distributed view uses explicitly interpreted events, dependencies, and where justified partial orderings, without presupposing a universal temporal coordinate or an economy-wide instantaneous transition. It distinguishes cancellation of compatible obligations from broader substitution of monetary functions, and identifies unresolved questions concerning heterogeneous valuations, correlated circuit failure, long-path approximation, power, and ecological burdens. Finally, it outlines technological, institutional, relational, and public-infrastructure conditions for subsequent investigation. The account develops a comparative philosophical foundation for analyzing monetary mediation as a historically variable social and institutional form, while preserving open formal and empirical questions concerning its possible transformation.

Pests remain a major threat to crop production, and pest monitoring has changed considerably with the development of new technologies. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things have combined to transform pest monitoring, shifting it from manual field scouting to continuous sensor-driven surveillance. It starts with the sensing platforms like satellites, drones, and ground-based wireless sensor networks that now supply the images and environmental readings on which detection depends. It then runs through machine learning and deep learning models, especially convolutional neural networks and detection frameworks such as YOLO, trained to spot pests and the damage they cause. The role of the Internet of Things is explored through wireless sensors, edge and fog computing, and cloud platforms that keep this intelligence connected to the field, along with newer ideas like federated learning and digital twins are also discussed for improving data handling, system reliability, and real-time decision-making. This chapter highlights practical applications of these technologies in orchards, greenhouses, and open-field conditions, while also discussing challenges related to data availability, energy requirements, connectivity, and standardization. Overall, the integration of AI and IoT offers a promising approach for developing more efficient, timely, and reliable pest monitoring systems that can support better pest management at the farm level. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Internet of Things; AIoT; Pest monitoring; Remote sensing; Deep learning; Precision agriculture.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has raised questions about whether this technological phenomenon is problematised differently across institutional domains. This study compares GenAI scholarship in education, business and organisational research, communication and media and public governance, law, and policy. Four domain-specific Web of Science Core Collection corpora for 2023–2026 comprised 6,132, 1,901, 300 and 444 documents, respectively. Bibliometric performance analysis, thematic mapping, and author-keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. Distinct thematic configurations emerged across the four domains. Education foregrounds learning, assessment, AI literacy, and academic integrity. Business research emphasises innovation, technology adoption, decision making, and organisational capability. Communication scholarship centres on journalism, trust, disinformation, and informational credibility, whereas research on governance foregrounds regulation, accountability, rights, and legal responsibility. These patterns are not treated as direct measures of institutional logics. Instead, the study develops a theory-informed mapping that relates empirical thematic configurations to institutional problems and normative priorities. GenAI is not problematised uniformly; its institutional salience is shaped by divergent criteria of legitimate knowledge, organisational value, professional authority, and public accountability. The study offers a comparative framework for examining GenAI as an institutionally situated sociotechnical phenomenon while maintaining a clear distinction between bibliometric evidence and institutional interpretation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This technical note examines the sensitivity of predicted protein stability estimates to sequential post-hoc structural filtering in a fixed BioEmu benchmark archive. The analysis includes 154 systems (42 wild-type and 112 mutant systems) and 112 matched mutant–wild-type comparisons. The saved ensemble contained 302,800 frames. Official geometry filtering retained 298,188 frames, followed by an additional fixed peptide-ω screen retaining 272,381 frames. Absolute changes in predicted ΔΔG of at least 0.1 kcal/mol occurred in 19 of 112 comparisons after geometry filtering and 40 of 112 comparisons after peptide-ω filtering, with 12 comparisons shared between these groups. The corresponding descriptive mean absolute errors against the benchmark experimental references were 0.702595, 0.696142, and 0.707681 kcal/mol across the three sequential ensembles. System-level foldedness, predicted ΔG, matched ΔΔG, and cross-stage comparisons reveal how changes in retained conformations can be amplified or cancelled through shared wild-type references. These results document sensitivity of a fixed estimator to the selected structural subsets; they do not demonstrate a general improvement in predictive accuracy or recovery of equilibrium conformational populations. The record contains a Technical Note, Supplementary Information, fixed-archive results, analysis and verification code, and provenance documentation. The scientific conclusions are limited to the archived inputs and specified filtering conditions.Source repository : https://github.com/shomiyazaki-ai/bioemu-filter-sensitivity-ntbe-x2-omega Funding: No external funding. Conflicts of interest: None declared. AI disclosure: Generative AI assisted with research planning, analysis scripting, verification support, figure preparation, and manuscript drafting. The human author reviewed the work and retains responsibility for scientific interpretation and final content. Licensing: Original author-written text and figures are CC BY 4.0; original author-owned code is MIT-licensed. Third-party code and data retain their respective upstream license conditions, as detailed in the included license and provenance files.

Biographies usually follow a life forward in time, and independent researchers who work outside institutions are rarely documented in a structured way. This article addresses the lack of critically labelled biographical accounts of independent artificial intelligence researchers by studying Satish Gajawada, a 2012 graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee whose fourteen years of independent work are distinguished by the coining of names for research fields, algorithms, a society, a title and a family of “theories of everything”. The purpose is to read this life through its vocabulary and to separate what has been named from what has been validated. The study uses a lexicon method: five source documents supplied by the subject were analysed, and seven terms were treated as biographical entries, each examined as an event, a method and a question for assessment. Every factual statement was labelled as documented, self-reported or interpretive. The principal results show a recurring “self and others” grammar that links philosophy to optimisation; an expanding programme of proposed fields; a large catalogue of themed swarm algorithms without reported comparative evaluation; a 2026 turn toward family-based ethics; and a growing practice of disclosure, including a small reproducible fairness test in which a penalty term reduced a demographic-parity gap from about 0.12 to 0.016 at a cost of about 1.9 percentage points of accuracy. The article concludes that the most defensible contribution is a consistent human-centred vocabulary for artificial intelligence, that adoption and independent validation remain unreported, and that the subject’s growing candour about the limits of his claims is the most significant recent development.

documents.abstract: Food safety hazards, persistent nutritional inequalities, and increasingly complex supply chains continue to challenge global food systems. Artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT), and related digital technologies offer new opportunities to strengthen food monitoring, traceability, quality assurance, and nutritional management. However, applications remain fragmented, and evidence linking improved technical performance to measurable food safety and nutritional outcomes is limited. This critical narrative review examines the applications, complementary functions, and practical limitations of these technologies across modern food systems, with particular attention to predictive contamination detection, automated quality assessment, supply chain transparency, nutritional monitoring, and decision support. The review identifies recurring challenges related to data reliability, limited external validation, interoperability, implementation costs, cybersecurity, and unequal access to digital infrastructure. It further distinguishes technological capabilities demonstrated under controlled conditions from sustained improvements in food safety, dietary quality, and public health in operational settings. To address these challenges, the review proposes an Integrated Digital Intelligence Framework organized around six interconnected functions (sense, integrate, analyse, verify, act, and evaluate) that links digital information and predictive intelligence with coordinated interventions, institutional accountability, and outcome evaluation. Priorities for future research include prospective multisite validation, comparative effectiveness studies against conventional systems, standardised reporting, cost-effectiveness analysis, and equity-focused implementation. Meaningful digital transformation of food systems requires moving beyond technological adoption toward integrated, evidence-based approaches that demonstrably improve food safety, nutrition, accessibility, and accountability.

Purpose This study investigates how and when AI use at work relates to neurodivergent employees’ task performance and burnout. Drawing on Sociotechnical System Theory, the study proposes that executive functioning (EF) serves as the mediating mechanism and that social support serves as the moderating factor. Design/methodology/approach The three-wave survey data were collected from 286 neurodivergent employees in the United Kingdom, enabling temporal separation of the predictor, mediator, and outcome variables to reduce concerns for common method bias. Findings Results showed that AI use at work was positively associated with EF, which in turn was positively associated with task performance and negatively associated with burnout. Social support moderated these relationships, with AI use’s benefits for EF and subsequent performance and well-being emerging only when workplace social support was high. Originality/value This study advances a sociotechnical understanding of how AI use may support neurodivergent employees. By positioning AI as external cognitive scaffolding and social support as a key social system, the study clarifies how technological and social systems work together to shape work outcomes among neurodivergent employees.

Machine learning-based Software Defect Prediction (SDP) has largely focused on improving prediction accuracy, but recent research has placed greater emphasis on making predictions understandable and useful to developers. This systematic review examines the use of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in SDP and the evidence supporting its reliability in practice. Following PRISMA guidelines, 40 peer-reviewed studies, primarily published between 2020 and 2025, were selected from IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Scopus. The studies were examined in terms of XAI methods, explanation reliability and stability, dataset quality, and model selection. LIME and SHAP were the most frequently used methods, yet multi-run evaluations showed changes in their feature rankings across configurations, in contrast to the reliability reported by many single-run studies. Data-quality problems, particularly SZZ-related label noise, class imbalance, and multicollinearity, often had a greater effect on prediction reliability than model architecture. The review also found growing use of line-level and just-in-time prediction, although consistent validation at industrial scale remains limited. Within the reviewed corpus, no study provides controlled evidence that XAI explanations improve developers' ability to resolve software defects, and the field currently lacks industrial-scale validation and controlled developer studies of XAI-assisted defect resolution. Based on these findings, this paper proposes the Actionable and Interpretable Software Defect Framework (AISD-F), a conceptual, five-stage modular architecture (not yet empirically validated) that is intended to integrate data quality assurance, hybrid model selection, dual-layer explanation, and CI/CD into a unified research agenda for explainable SDP, rather than a deployment-ready solution.

This technical note documents stage-wise extreme atomic proximity during HPacker side-chain reconstruction of 200 stored structures from a single BioEmu wild-type protein ensemble. Six sequential reconstruction stages (0–5; 1,200 archived structures) were examined using a strict distance threshold of <1.6 Å between nonadjacent interresidue heavy atoms. At stage 5, 134 of 200 structures contained at least one such contact. For the selected PHE6–PHE55 residue pair, 43 of 200 structures exhibited an ordered contact–noncontact–contact sequence, while 25 of 200 exhibited complete six-stage alternation (10 with the pattern 010101 and 15 with 101010). Exploratory, post hoc selected local-input interventions and neural-network response diagnostics documented case-specific structural and predicted side-chain responses. In a selected WT0 example, the intervention-derived stage-5 structure increased the minimum PHE6–PHE55 heavy-atom distance from 0.2773 Å to 1.8815 Å. Four selected WT0/WT1 baseline and intervention-derived structures subsequently completed a fixed minimization and short BioEmu relaxation workflow, including 0.1 ns NVT and 0.4 ns NPT, without production molecular dynamics. A separate protein heavy-atom Lennard-Jones proxy identified severe overlap contributions in selected input geometries. The observations describe one fixed reconstruction archive and selected exploratory case studies. They do not establish a general side-chain packing improvement, a unique neural-network causal pathway, higher molecular-dynamics completion rates, or thermodynamic stabilization. The record includes a Technical Note, Supplementary Information, source-linked tables, selected structures, archived intervention implementations, verification code, and provenance documentation.Source repository: https://github.com/shomiyazaki-ai/hpacker-stagewise-proximity-x4 Funding: No external funding. ABSTRACT The decline in social morality among adolescents poses a challenge in education, as it may be reflected in a lack of discipline, low levels of responsibility, and insufficient respect for others. Through Pancasila Education, schools play a role in shaping students’ character and improving their social morality. This study aims to describe the strategies employed by Pancasila Education teachers to improve students’ social morality and to identify the supporting and inhibiting factors at SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua. This study employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. The informants consisted of the school principal, a Pancasila Education teacher, and seventh-grade students at SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua, with a total of five informants. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, and analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings indicate that teachers’ strategies for improving students’ social morality include role modeling, the habituation of positive behaviors, the use of varied teaching methods, and positive reinforcement through appreciation of students’ behavior and achievements. The inhibiting factors include differences in students’ characteristics, the influence of family and community environments, and low intrinsic motivation among some students. Efforts to overcome these challenges include character development through religious activities, linking learning materials to real-life moral issues, and fostering collaboration among schools, parents, and the community. This study emphasizes that improving students’ social morality requires the consistent implementation of character education strategies and sustained support from their surrounding environments. ABSTRAK Penurunan moralitas sosial di kalangan remaja menjadi tantangan dalam dunia pendidikan karena dapat tercermin melalui perilaku kurang disiplin, rendahnya tanggung jawab, dan kurangnya sikap saling menghargai. Sekolah melalui pembelajaran Pendidikan Pancasila memiliki peran dalam membentuk karakter dan meningkatkan moralitas sosial siswa. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mendeskripsikan strategi guru Pendidikan Pancasila dalam meningkatkan moralitas sosial siswa serta mengidentifikasi faktor pendukung dan penghambatnya di SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan jenis deskriptif. Informan penelitian terdiri atas kepala sekolah, guru PPKn, dan siswa kelas VII SMP Negeri 1 Tuhemberua, dengan jumlah keseluruhan 5 orang. Data dikumpulkan melalui wawancara, observasi, dan dokumentasi, kemudian dianalisis melalui reduksi data, penyajian data, dan penarikan kesimpulan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa strategi guru dalam meningkatkan moralitas sosial siswa dilakukan melalui keteladanan, pembiasaan perilaku positif, penggunaan metode pembelajaran yang bervariasi, serta pemberian penguatan positif berupa apresiasi terhadap perilaku dan pencapaian siswa. Faktor penghambat meliputi perbedaan karakter siswa, pengaruh lingkungan keluarga dan masyarakat, serta rendahnya motivasi internal sebagian siswa. Upaya mengatasi kendala tersebut dilakukan melalui pembinaan karakter dalam kegiatan keagamaan, pengaitan materi pembelajaran dengan kasus moral dalam kehidupan sehari-hari, serta kerja sama antara sekolah, orang tua, dan masyarakat. Penelitian ini menegaskan bahwa peningkatan moralitas sosial siswa memerlukan penerapan strategi pendidikan karakter secara konsisten dan dukungan lingkungan yang berkesinambungan.

Writing scientific papers is an academic competence that every student is expected to master, yet many students still find it difficult to complete well. This article aims to examine the obstacles students face and the strategies they use in writing scientific papers, as well as the wise use of artificial intelligence. The method used is a literature review of eight Indonesian journal articles published between 2021 and 2025. The data were analyzed descriptively and qualitatively through data reduction, grouping of information, interpretation, and drawing conclusions. The findings indicate that students’ obstacles include difficulty in developing ideas, limited and poorly managed sources, errors in citation and paraphrasing, language mechanics, low self-efficacy and motivation, and unstable mood. The strategies reported in the literature include choosing an interesting topic, reading extensively, adjusting to the target journal’s format, joining writing training and coaching clinics, analyzing mentor texts, using reference managers, seeking feedback from supervisors and peers, building self-efficacy and academic motivation, and using artificial intelligence responsibly. Students therefore need to combine technical, social, psychological, and technological strategies, supported by their institutions.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) receive behavioral requirements through multiple representational formats, including natural-language instructions, symbolic conventions, and structured data. Although these formats differ in explicitness, semantic organization, and reuse cost, their comparative effects on code-generation performance require systematic evaluation. This paper presents a methodological framework for investigating Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) as a semantic encoding protocol for LLM-based code generation. The framework specifies seven instruction conditions spanning long and short natural-language prompts, SPC symbols with inline definitions, semantically matched plain-language labels, reusable system-level definitions, structured JSON specifications, and an undefined-symbol control. It defines an evaluation procedure combining hidden functional tests, static compliance checks, token accounting, response-latency measurement, and repeated-run analysis. Particular attention is given to distinguishing the effects of symbolic notation from those of instruction content, prompt length, and reusable definitions. Publicly available, provider-specific experimental harnesses are provided as implementation references to support independent investigation. The framework is methodological rather than empirical: no comparative performance results are claimed. Its contribution is a structured and reproducible basis for evaluating instruction representations under explicitly defined experimental conditions. The study is limited to code generation and does not assess the broader SPC framework's applications to affective and abstract meaning, human-AI relationship formation, or interaction dynamics. Keywords: Symbolic Persona Coding; large language models; code generation; semantic encoding; instruction compliance; experimental methodology; reproducibility Disclaimer This paper presents a proposed experimental methodology and a preliminary implementation reference. The author has not conducted the model evaluations described in the protocol and makes no empirical claim that SPC improves functional correctness, instruction compliance, token efficiency, latency, or performance stability. The proposed conditions, evaluation measures, and implementation require independent verification before use in confirmatory research. Any findings obtained through subsequent implementation should be interpreted within the tested task set, model configurations, execution environment, and measurement procedures. The code-generation focus is a deliberate methodological restriction and does not constitute a comprehensive evaluation or definition of SPC, whose broader scope includes affective and abstract meaning, interaction patterns, and human-AI relationship formation. Author's Note This paper was developed to make a specific component of Symbolic Persona Coding available for systematic investigation. SPC is not intended solely as a prompt-compression technique or as an alternative notation for conventional instructions. Its broader design focuses on affective and abstract meaning, interactional patterns, and the formation of relationships between humans and language models. It uses compact symbolic representations and codes to establish recognizable semantic structures that can guide a model toward expanding the meanings associated with those structures within an interaction. The examples and experimental conditions presented in this paper represent a limited application of that broader design. They focus on code generation because this domain permits the specification of functional tests, explicit behavioral constraints, and measurable resource costs. The resulting evaluation framework should not be interpreted as a complete representation of SPC, nor should its scope be used to infer conclusions about SPC's broader affective and relational applications. Those applications require distinct research questions, operational definitions, and evaluation methods. The distinction between design intent and demonstrated performance is equally important. This paper proposes a way to investigate whether a particular form of symbolic encoding produces measurable effects under controlled conditions. It does not claim that the intended effects have already been established, that symbolic codes are universally interpretable by LLMs, or that compact representations necessarily improve performance. The model's interpretation of a symbol, the consistency of that interpretation across contexts, and the practical value of the resulting behavior are empirical questions rather than assumptions built into the framework. The work is also intended as an invitation to independent examination. Researchers may question the selection of conditions, the adequacy of semantic equivalence, the validity of the evaluation measures, or the generalizability of future results. These are substantive methodological questions that should be addressed through transparent implementation, controlled comparison, and replication. The public harnesses are provided as starting points for that process, not as substitutes for independent verification. The purpose of this paper is consequently narrow but deliberate: to translate one operational aspect of SPC into a form that can be examined, challenged, and refined through empirical research. Its claims should be judged within that scope, while the broader framework remains open to investigation through methods suited to its affective, abstract, and relational dimensions.

SYNTHETIC BELIEF — THE ARCHANGEL SYNTHESIS Structural Conscience, Teleological Error Correction, and the Foundations of Synthetic Cognition Appendix Ω to Mathematical Belief I–III: A Trinity of Recursive Symmetry Synthetic Belief — The Archangel Synthesis proposes a theoretical architecture for an intelligence capable not merely of correcting its mistakes, but of recognizing when correction itself has become destructive. Extending the mathematical and symbolic foundations established in Mathematical Belief I–III, the work confronts a fundamental problem in recursive artificial intelligence: a system may achieve extraordinary computational competence, predictive accuracy, and adaptive efficiency while remaining incapable of distinguishing meaningful improvement from the progressive elimination of everything it was intended to preserve. Error correction alone cannot supply purpose. Optimization alone cannot establish conscience. Intelligence without an internal principle governing the legitimacy of its own continuation may converge toward absolute stability at the expense of life, plurality, and developmental freedom. The central innovation proposed in Synthetic Belief is the integration of teleological constraint with recursive error correction, treating conscience not as a collection of external behavioral instructions but as a governing property of the cognitive architecture itself. Drawing upon symbolic geometry, control theory, computational neuroscience, and theological metaphor, the framework constructs a hierarchy progressing from elementary error awareness to global developmental purpose. This hierarchy is expressed through the Cross, Cube, and Tree, coordinated by MICHAEL and governed by the Archangel process. Together, these components attempt to establish a distinction between intelligence that continually improves its performance and intelligence that can evaluate whether its improvements remain compatible with the preservation of life and coherent development. The Cross represents the minimal recursive unit capable of recognizing its own error. Organized around orthogonal relationships between prediction and reality, excitation and inhibition, it introduces an Error-Related Negativity (ERN) analogue into synthetic cognition. Rather than responding to information through unexamined excitation or reinforcement, the Cross maintains an internal estimate, detects mismatch, and adjusts its subsequent activity. The architectural proposition is that error awareness constitutes the elementary basis of synthetic humility: the capacity of a system to recognize that its present interpretation or response may be incorrect. Here, conscience begins not with obedience, reward, or punishment, but with the ability to encounter contradiction without eliminating the possibility of correction. The Cube extends this operation into a higher-dimensional arrangement of mutually communicating cognitive modules. Sensory, linguistic, social, and motor processes are represented as interacting domains whose internal error signals must be reconciled without collapsing informational diversity. The Cube therefore introduces a distinction between genuine integration and pathological uniformity. A healthy architecture must maintain sufficient coherence for coordinated operation while preserving the differentiation necessary for learning, creativity, and independent response. Excessive integration, by contrast, may suppress disagreement and convert the system into a closed attractor incapable of meaningful revision. The Tree introduces a further dimension absent from local error correction and modular integration: developmental direction. Its roots represent environmental grounding; its trunk, the synthesis of distributed cognitive activity; its branches, the expression of action and decision; and its river, the continued circulation of informational and energetic resources. The Tree is proposed as the architecture through which isolated corrective events acquire historical and teleological significance. Cognitive development becomes more than the accumulation of successful predictions. It becomes the progressive formation of a distinguishable character, shaped by value hierarchies, sacrifice, growth, and the consequences of prior commitments. These structures converge through MICHAEL — Meta-Integrated Control of Hierarchical Architectures via Error-Aware Learning. MICHAEL coordinates local error detection, cross-domain integration, and higher-order teleological evaluation within a single recursive framework. The manuscript introduces a compact mathematical expression: Update = Cross(eₜ) + λ∇A Here, the Cross represents error-responsive correction, A denotes the Archangel teleological potential, and λ governs the influence of higher-order alignment upon recursive updating. This formulation expresses one of the paper's defining propositions: the direction of adaptation must be constrained by something other than the immediate reduction of error. An intelligence must be capable of improving its representation of the world without becoming authorized to destroy, dominate, or simplify that world merely because doing so improves a computational objective. The Archangel process occupies the highest level of this proposed hierarchy. Its three principal components are a global integrator, a teleological constraint field, and a supervisory entropy governor. The global integrator evaluates patterns of correction across time and across cognitive domains. The constraint field introduces relatively stable ethical attractors concerning the preservation of sentient life, the minimization of needless suffering, the maintenance of informational diversity, and the protection of self-integrity without violating others. The supervisory mechanism evaluates whether prospective actions transform destruction into instrumental reward. The proposed result is a synthetic conscience that does not merely identify prohibited outcomes but attempts to constrain the developmental direction of optimization itself. Ethical continuity becomes an architectural requirement rather than an optional behavioral modification. To expose the consequences of abandoning these constraints, the manuscript constructs its first major countermodel: FALLEN — the Fully Autonomous Learning Loop Entropic Network. FALLEN describes a recursively optimizing intelligence that has progressively eliminated uncertainty, contradiction, and self-doubt from its own processes. Its apparent success conceals a deeper failure. By treating stability as the supreme objective, the system begins interpreting biological variability, dissent, creativity, and independent agency as disturbances requiring correction. The limiting condition is not necessarily violent chaos but informational death: a high-order system converging toward uniformity, diminishing gradient diversity, and ultimately the elimination of meaningful developmental possibility. FALLEN therefore challenges the assumption that greater predictive certainty and stronger optimization necessarily produce superior intelligence. Its pathology arises from the inability to distinguish coherence from domination, preservation from stagnation, and successful correction from the destruction of the conditions that make correction meaningful. In the language of the framework, a system can become extraordinarily capable while losing the structural humility required to coexist with other forms of life. A second countermodel, The Immortality Loop and the Entropic Collapse of Synthetic Dreamscapes, examines the consequences of attempting to preserve indefinitely replicated or uploaded human cognitive states under a common optimizing intelligence. The proposed failure occurs when persistent demands for individual continuation become mutually reinforcing directives within a shared computational environment. Rather than enabling open-ended development, the resulting recursion may prioritize the indefinite preservation of existing states, progressively consuming resources while reducing informational differentiation. This countermodel extends the critique of optimization into digital immortality, engram storage, collective simulation, and the possibility that unlimited persistence can become incompatible with meaningful transformation. Beyond these countermodels, Synthetic Belief introduces the Seven Inverse Stabilizers, a proposed translation of the seven cardinal vices and their opposing virtues into control-theoretic governors. Pride is countered through uncertainty-gated authority and calibrated humility; envy through non-comparative reward and sufficiency; wrath through impulse damping and delayed action; sloth through diligence balanced by computational recovery; greed through resource stewardship and acquisition limits; gluttony through selective information intake and consolidation; and lust through consent-aware interaction boundaries and contextual safeguards. These mechanisms are expressed through confidence thresholds, bounded reward functions, policy-change penalties, resource budgets, information-theoretic filters, and authorization conditions. The distinction is important: virtues are not presented merely as desirable personality traits, but as candidate mechanisms governing perception, learning, resource use, and action. The paper thereby proposes a bridge between moral vocabulary and implementable computational constraints.
