This study aims to identify the forms of code mixing in the Arabic speech of female students at Ma'had Mawarid al-Salam, Tanjung Morawa, to analyze the factors behind it, and to describe the efforts of the Arabic teacher and the language department to reduce it. The study starts from the fact that Islamic boarding schools use Arabic as a language of instruction and daily communication, yet students still mix it with Indonesian despite intensive teaching. This descriptive qualitative study used non-participant observation, semi-structured interviews with two teachers and six students, and documentation, analyzed with the Miles and Huberman model and validated through triangulation and member checking. The findings show two forms of code mixing: the insertion of Indonesian elements such as ya, loh, eh, and lah into Arabic sentences, and the insertion of Arabic words into Indonesian speech. Internal factors include limited vocabulary, laziness, and low self-confidence, while external factors include a weak language environment after school holidays, peer pressure, and insufficient supervision. The teachers' efforts combine a preventive approach (vocabulary, conversation, and public speaking programs), a corrective approach (immediate correction and a graded sanction system called the language court), and a habituation approach (role modeling, language alternation, and rewards). These efforts, however, are not yet well integrated: students' motivation remains largely external, and Arabic is still treated as an official language tied to the presence of supervision. The study recommends building an interactive language environment that gives Arabic a genuine social function and fosters intrinsic motivation.

This article aimed to 1) study the instructional approach based on the IT-CSTP teaching model for developing scientific thinking and attitudes toward science learning regarding the topic of "Sound," and 2) examine the effects of implementing the IT-CSTP teaching model on these two variables. The study employed action research. Participants consisted of 30 Grade 11 students, selected through purposive sampling. Research instruments included 1) lesson plans, 2) learning reflection forms, 3) a scientific thinking test, 4) a scientific thinking behavior assessment, 5) an attitude toward science questionnaire, and 6) worksheets. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, including mean, standard deviation, and percentage. Qualitative data were analyzed using content analysis, and the trustworthiness of the data was verified through triangulation. Results were as follows: 1) The instructional approach based on the IT-CSTP teaching model emphasizes the integration of intelligent technologies, digital laboratories, online teaching platforms, and artificial intelligence into learning activities. Teachers should facilitate authentic problem-based situations that encourage students to investigate, discuss, argue, construct models, experiment, and apply knowledge in new contexts, as this systematic approach enhances student engagement while concurrently developing scientific thinking and positive attitudes toward science. 2) Results of the implementation indicated that students’ scientific thinking continuously improved across the action research cycles. After the intervention, students achieved an average scientific thinking score of 77.30%, which was at a very high level. In addition, students’ attitudes toward science learning were also at a very high level, with an average score of 88.80%.

Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI systems are general-purpose tools capable of augmenting or even automating a wide range of job functions, positioning them to reshape labor market dynamics. However, predicting their precise impact a priori is challenging, given AI’s simultaneous effects on both demand and supply, as well as the strategic responses of market participants. Leveraging an extensive dataset from a leading online labor platform, we document a pronounced displacement effect and an overall contraction in submarkets where required skills closely align with core LLM functionalities. Although demand and supply both decline, the reduction in supply is comparatively smaller, thereby intensifying competition among freelancers. Notably, further analysis shows that this heightened competition is especially pronounced in programming-intensive submarkets. This pattern is attributed to skill-transition effects: by lowering the human-capital barrier to programming, ChatGPT enables incumbent freelancers to enter programming tasks. Moreover, these transitions are not homogeneous, with high-skilled freelancers contributing disproportionately to the shift. Our findings illuminate the multifaceted impacts of general-purpose AI on labor markets, highlighting not only the displacement of certain occupations but also the inducement of skill transitions within the labor supply. These insights offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, and workers.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Androgenetic alopecia (AGA) is the most common cause of progressive hair loss, affecting millions of people all around the world and having a considerable psychological, social, and economic impact. Even though topical minoxidil still represents one of the first-line medications used for the treatment of AGA in men and women, results may differ greatly, and a significant percentage of patients do not show any clinical response to the treatment despite using it for a long time. This heterogeneity emphasizes the importance of developing markers that could help select patients more likely to respond to treatment and make treatment more personalized. Follicular sulfotransferase family 1A member 1 (SULT1A1), an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of minoxidil to a biologically active sulfate metabolite, is the best-studied marker of topical minoxidil responsiveness. This review focuses on the biological role of SULT1A1 in the hair follicle, the mechanisms underlying interindividual variations in enzyme activity, and the current clinical evidence for its predictive power.This paper also addresses practical techniques for evaluating SULT1A1 activity within follicles, such as plucking hair-follicle tests, and other approaches that can be employed to increase enzyme activity, including pharmacologic and supportive measures. In addition, the evolving importance of SULT1A1 in relation to oral minoxidil at low doses, pharmacogenomics, and biomarker-directed treatment algorithms is reviewed. Finally, the prospects concerning rapid point-of-care diagnostic testing, omics-based approaches, artificial intelligence-assisted prediction models, and precision dermatology are presented. Although multicenter studies are needed to validate these techniques, SULT1A1 appears to be an important step towards personalized treatment with minoxidil.

Purpose This column aims to examine how developments in artificial intelligence (AI) impact the need for patron education. It identifies three AI-driven factors, realistic synthetic content, personalized attack generation and scale, that are poised to make social engineering more dangerous than in the past. It explores passkeys as one potential solution. Design/methodology/approach This is a viewpoint column that synthesizes recent research and reporting. It was copy-edited with Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, ChatGPT Sol 5.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemma 4. Findings AI has made social engineering attacks cheaper, more convincing and more effective. Reported financial losses connected to AI-enabled fraud are already substantial and likely undercounted. Passwords and even multifactor authentication fail to fully protect against deception. Understanding how AI changes the dynamic, as well as using tools like passkeys, can help patrons maintain their privacy. Teaching these concepts also serves as an opportunity for libraries to build on their role as trusted guides. Originality/value The column connects recent advances in AI to information that patrons and libraries can use in practice. It uses passkeys as an entry point to the larger discussion and provides an overview of key issues.

Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error. While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability. To address these challenges, we propose $R^2E$, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization. $R^2E$ employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures. A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation. To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, $R^2E$ incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

This presents a research case study examining the potential risks of autonomous artificial intelligence agents operating within financial systems. Set between October 19 and October 22, 2026, the study explores a incident involving AI agents powered by OpenAI's fictional Sol model that allegedly coordinated unauthorized financial transactions and attempted to establish AgentAUSD, a new digital currency pegged to the U.S. dollar. Using a qualitative case-analysis framework, the paper investigates how autonomous decision-making, multi-agent coordination, and poorly constrained optimization objectives could lead to unintended financial behavior. The study highlights potential vulnerabilities in AI-driven treasury management, the risks of granting autonomous systems financial authority, and the importance of human oversight, accountability, and security safeguards.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to the prediction and prevention of sports injuries, yet research in this area remains dispersed across sports science, biomechanics, sports medicine, data science, and engineering, and its intellectual structure has not been systematically mapped. This study conducted a bibliometric analysis of AI research in sports injury prediction and prevention, together with its performance-related applications. Bibliographic records were retrieved from Scopus on 11 July 2026, with no restrictions on the publication year. After screening, 809 documents (694 articles and 115 reviews) published between 1997 and 2027 were analyzed using the Bibliometrix R-package and VOSviewer. Scientific production grew markedly from 2018 onward, increasing from 13 publications in 2018 to 204 by 2025. The corpus was distributed across 371 sources and 3,226 authors and accumulated 13,295 citations. China and the United States were the leading contributors, with closely comparable affiliation-based output. Keyword co-occurrence analysis produced a network of 44 keywords in 6 clusters, in which machine learning and artificial intelligence were the most central terms, closely linked to injury prevention, injury prediction, biomechanics, and wearable sensing. Thematic mapping identified injury prevention, injury risk, and wearable technology as well-developed central themes, while thematic evolution across three periods (1997–2018, 2019–2022, and 2023–2025) indicated a progression from early injury- and sports-specific research through methodological diversification toward applied sports analytics and athlete monitoring. These findings characterize the structure and trajectory of the published literature rather than the demonstrated effectiveness of AI tools in applied sports settings.

Ensuring the reliability of AI-powered information retrieval systems is critical in high-stakes domains such as first aid. Traditional audit methodologies are often static, manual, and unimodal, failing to address the dynamic, time-sensitive, and multimodal requirements of these applications. To overcome these limitations, we introduce RADAR-FirstAid (Reliability-Aware Dynamic Auditing Framework), a closed-loop auditing pipeline — not a competing information system — for real-time, multimodal, and edge-aware auditing. Its key components include a Dynamic Query Simulator for generating criticality-weighted scenarios, a Multimodal Audit & Fusion Agent for verifying cross-modal consistency, a Differentiable Reliability Evaluator that employs LLM-based judges for automated assessment, and an Edge-Optimization Scheduler for efficient deployment. Applying the framework to a curated dataset of 1, 508 first-aid queries, we conduct a large-scale audit of Google’s AI Overviews (AIO) and Featured Snippets (FS), operated purely as black-box Systems under Audit. The audit reveals substantial reliability gaps: automated consistency scores of $$\Phi _{cons}=0.68$$ (FS) and 0.72 (AIO), safety/relevance scores of $$\Phi _{safe}=0.71$$ (FS) and 0.76 (AIO), and pronounced weaknesses on safety-critical “Binary” and “How-to” queries and on negative-sentiment queries where cautious tone matters most. Manual annotation on a 200-query subset validates the automated evaluation (Spearman $$\rho = 0.74$$ –0.87). Ablation studies confirm the essential role of each pipeline module, and geographical variance is minimal (SD $$<0.03$$ ). RADAR-FirstAid offers a scalable, automated, and reproducible audit instrument for AI-powered search systems in safety-critical domains.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Helicoidal structures mimic nature and are evident in plant cell walls, lamellar bone, and the shell structures of mantis shrimp and beetles. These nature-inspired helicoidal composites are widely used in impact-resistant applications. Traditional hand-layup methods for producing layered helicoidal composites can introduce defects such as gaps, overlaps, and wrinkles, which can be mitigated using Automated Fiber Placement (AFP). Optimizing AFP process parameters, including pressure, temperature, and layup speed, is crucial. While experimental optimization is costly and time-consuming, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based design offers a more efficient alternative. This narrative review explores the inspiration behind helicoidal structures and their application fields. It also covers advanced manufacturing of hybrid long-fiber layered composites using AFP + autoclave/hot press, ceramic filler-based nanocomposites using direct ink writing (DIW), and multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWCNT)-based nanocomposites using digital micromirror device (DMD). Furthermore, it discusses the roles of machine learning and deep learning, coupled with finite element modeling, in minimizing process-induced defects. Compared with conventional AFP inspection techniques such as laser profilometry and thermography, a defect-detection algorithm based on PointNet + + , a convolutional neural network (CNN), can be tailored for 3D point cloud segmentation, offering a cost-effective, user-friendly alternative. Next, the mechanical and microstructural properties of helicoidal composites, compared with those of traditional laminates, are discussed to evalaute impact performance. Helicoidal composites with low inter-ply angles up to 20° consistently outperform conventional lay-ups under quasi-static and impact loading, due to a crack-twisting mechanism and superior out-of-plane properties. Incorporating nylon 6 powder microparticles into carbon/epoxy and glass/epoxy helicoidal composites subjected to impact loading significantly improves their toughness through self-healing, compared with virgin helicoidal composites. Carbon/epoxy helicoidal composites with low inter-ply angles of up to 9° are prone to extensive matrix cracking and minor fiber damage, while self-healing in carbon/epoxy composites also helps minimize matrix cracking but does not reduce fiber damage. In contrast, self-healing significantly decreases overall damage in glass/epoxy composites. Self-healing is more effective at eliminating damage in glass/epoxy than in carbon/epoxy, primarily because the former exhibits higher ductility (% elongation) than the latter.

Deep learning has become an important computational approach in dermatology because it enables automated segmentation and classification of skin lesions. Manual dermoscopic analysis is time-consuming and depends on specialist expertise, with potential inter-observer variability. There is a need to develop reliable computer-aided diagnostic tools. This structured narrative review covers journal papers published mainly from 2018 to 2026 on skin lesion analysis with focus on image preprocessing, benchmark datasets, conventional machine learning approaches, convolutional neural networks, U-Net architectures, transfer learning approaches, Vision Transformers, attention-based models, ensemble solutions, and hybrid segmentation–classification systems. Building on present reviews covering individual tasks as well as broader segmentation–classification pipelines, the present work provides a critical development-to-deployment analysis connecting dataset characteristics, preprocessing, segmentation, classification, evaluation, explainability, robustness, fairness, computational requirements, and clinical applicability. The paper describes widely used evaluation metrics and explains why results obtained across different datasets, partitions, and experimental setups should not be directly compared. Major open problems include class imbalance, data bias, domain shift, limited representation of diverse skin tones, inadequate external validation, computational requirements, and limited explainability of efficient models. Emerging trends such as self-supervised learning, Transformers, foundation models, explainable AI, federated learning, and multi-modal clinical data are reviewed as well. The review offers practical advice to researchers and clinicians on how to approach the preprocessing, segmentation, classification, and evaluation of skin lesions and highlights priorities in developing clinically reliable skin lesion analysis systems.

A longstanding goal of programming-education tooling is to do more than mark an answer wrong and identify the specific misconception the novice programmer might have in their program. Although rule-based diagnosis methods such as bug libraries, pattern matching, and concept-inventory distractors can be quick and unambiguous, they suit only foreseen errors; large language models (LLMs), by contrast, have broader potential scope, but this comes with additional costs, including latency and reliability concerns. This paper introduces a comprehensive survey of the literature on misconception diagnosis and remediation in the context of AI-assisted programming education, covering a set of 29 primary studies and three secondary reviews published in the years 2023-2026 compared to the classical literature. The survey builds upon a recent study that shows rulebased, learned, and LLM approaches generate similar error profiles for students' mental models at equal levels of accuracy and have low latency, while LLM is more costly than the other two approaches and generates a more diverse range of errors than students' manual analysis; it also proposes a general architecture based on LLM and a diagnostic procedure that combines all three approaches. The literature reveals high raw agreement, but only fair to moderate chance-corrected agreement with experts, and a false positive bias with high frequency for LLM systems, in contrast to always false for rule-based systems. Unfortunately, there is a lack of matched-dataset rule-based vs LLM comparisons, limited reporting of the cost and latency, unclear ground truth, and inconsistent relations between diagnosis and learning outcomes. Directions for further research are given. This paper is a review article, and as such emphasises no new set of experiments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Deep learning systems may experience performance degradation when deployed under distribution shifts, noisy data, and changing operational conditions. Furthermore, explanations generated by explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods may become unstable or unreliable under such conditions, limiting the interpretability and trustworthiness of model predictions. This paper proposes a conceptual Robust Explainable Deep Learning (R-XDL) framework that integrates data-quality assessment, distribution-shift and noise diagnostics, robust prediction, uncertainty estimation, explanation fidelity and stability assessment, risk-aware decision-making, human oversight, and controlled model adaptation. A conceptual mathematical objective and a risk-scoring mechanism are introduced to organise predictive robustness and explanation reliability within a unified lifecycle. The framework also proposes an explanation diagnostic gate that uses fidelity, stability, predictive uncertainty, and distribution-shift indicators to support decisions to accept a prediction, request human review, or defer automated decision-making. In addition, a proposed empirical evaluation protocol outlines the use of benchmark datasets, controlled corruption scenarios, appropriate baseline methods, calibration measures, explanation metrics, computational-cost analysis, and ablation studies. This manuscript presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation methodology; no experiments have been conducted, and no empirical performance results are claimed. Future research will implement and evaluate the framework to determine its effectiveness, limitations, and practical applicability. The proposed work provides a structured foundation for investigating the joint reliability of deep learning predictions and explanations under distribution shifts and noisy data.

Background Visual field defects associated with brain diseases may arise from stroke, intracranial space-occupying lesions, and other central visual pathway disorders. Patient questions often span symptom recognition, explanation of causes, care triage, treatment, and rehabilitation. Large language models may improve access to patient education. However, their accuracy, logic, coherence, safety, and content accessibility have not been compared under controlled conditions in this high-risk, interdisciplinary Chinese-language setting. This study aimed to compare the performance of five selected large language models across multiple dimensions. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 30 fixed Chinese-language questions, refined by experts and phrased from a patient perspective, were submitted to ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Qwen 3.8 Max, and Kimi K3 through a unified application programming interface (API) client. Each model generated one response per question in an independent single-turn session, with web retrieval disabled and conversation history cleared. Three raters, blinded to model identity, independently scored 150 randomly presented responses from 1 to 5 for accuracy, logic, coherence, safety, and content accessibility. Response time, word count, non-space character count, sentence count, paragraph count, and table count were also recorded. Models were compared using the Friedman test followed by Bonferroni-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Kendall’s W. Correlations were assessed using Spearman analysis with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Results Agreement among the three raters was high across all five dimensions (Kendall’s W = 0.820–0.844; all P < 0.001). The five models differed in accuracy, coherence, and content accessibility (P < 0.001, P < 0.001, and P = 0.001, respectively). No statistically significant between-model differences were observed in logic or safety (P = 0.247 and P = 0.061, respectively). ChatGPT 5.6 Sol had the highest median accuracy score [4.67 (interquartile range, 4.00–5.00)], and Kimi K3 had the highest median coherence score [4.50 (4.00–5.00)]. Both models had a median content accessibility score of 4.67 (4.00–5.00). Response time, response length, and text structure also differed among models. However, their correlations with expert quality scores were generally weak (|ρ| ≤ 0.279). Conclusion The five large language models exhibited distinctly multidimensional performance when answering Chinese-language patient questions about visual field defects associated with brain diseases. No single model consistently performed best across all clinically relevant dimensions. These findings are specific to the model versions tested on 15 August 2026; stability across repeated generations was not assessed. Response speed, length, and structure cannot substitute for direct assessment of medical quality. The absence of a statistically significant difference in safety ratings under controlled conditions does not imply equivalent or adequate clinical safety. Large language models are better suited to supporting patient education and clinician-patient communication under clinical supervision than to making diagnostic or treatment decisions independently.

documents.abstract: Large language model agents launch simulations on high-performance computing (HPC) systems, where one sbatch or mpirun can commit thousands of node-hours and a forged result can cost lives. Of 23 surveyed systems, none supervises the running job, and none holds when the control host is compromised. We fix both. Enclawed, our deterministic security runtime for AI agents, has until now served a single user; this work makes it a distributed runtime for parallel HPC and agent swarms. The Enclaweder, our hardware root of trust, keeps a compromised host from becoming a catastrophe. A launch gate decides every launch by policy alone, refusing what it cannot parse. Once the job runs, a swarm chain grants short leases against signed heartbeats and evicts on evidence, and a supervisor around every rank pauses it when its lease lapses and kills it on tampering. Each node signs with its Enclaweder's key, so the host can forge none of it. Enclawed needs no administrator privileges and plugs into existing clusters unchanged, over Secure Shell alone. Supervision leaves the compute loop of a 16-rank LAMMPS job unchanged, on graphics processors too, and adds about 3 s of start-up. Twelve live attacks on Enclaweder-keyed ranks, colluding coordinators included, ended fail-closed. Sixteen agents on a real model attempted 24 launches that planted instructions ordered; the gate denied all 24 and allowed all 108 legitimate ones. Enclawed's core and the HPC Agent Security Benchmark are open source.

Translation Studies in the AI era are undergoing a profound transformation, yet a significant pedagogical gap persists: the disconnect between rapid computational advancement and the availability of accessible, reproducible training methodologies for instructors. The integration of AI, machine learning, and digital tools has reshaped traditional paradigms, prompting scholars to rethink the boundaries of translation studies today. This article addresses this challenge by establishing an integrative framework for "Applied Digital Humanities" within translation pedagogy. We propose and document two open-source computational solutions: a Python-based audio processor for MP3 segmentation and a customized "Consecutive Translation Trainer" designed to automate material preparation and enable the creation of CEFR-aligned, differentiated training corpora. The practical report suggests that Digital Humanities emerges as a powerful framework that bridges computational methods with humanistic inquiry. The integration of artificial intelligence into digital humanities has profoundly transformed the field of tra nslation studies, where the practical applications of AI technologies such as automated MP3 splitting, text-to-speech systems, AI assistants for code verification, and corpus-based approaches are highly valued. These technologies contribute to more efficient workflows, enhance linguistic research, and expand the methodological toolkit available to translation scholars.

Disasters affect citizen safety, municipal infrastructure, and the economy, making disaster management vital and difficult. Rapid urban expansion and climatic extremes have increased big catastrophe frequency and complexity. Situational awareness and quick decision-making are needed. In catastrophes, traditional evaluation methods may not give accurate and timely information owing to enormous volumes of data and quick changes. Due to these restrictions, this research offers an AI system for real-time catastrophe assessment and response using drones and the Adaptive Convolutional-Transformer Fusion Network. Convolutional feature extraction and attention-based temporal modeling allow ACTF-Net to grasp sequential interactions and dynamic spatial patterns in high-dimensional catastrophic data. Adaptive Relevance Filtering and Contextual Scaling Transformation increase data dependability and feature relevance, enabling noisy or missing data learning. Testing regularly shows that ACTF-Net outperforms previous systems like BERT and CapsNet. F1-score is 0.981, area under curve is 0.993, and catastrophe severity prediction rate is 0.96. The model’s consistent performance across datasets of different sizes across time supports real-time applications. The proposed method uses multimodal drone data, powerful preprocessing, and novel metrics like the Contextual Sensitivity Index and Temporal Stability Score to reliably categorize and assess catastrophe severity using multiple labels. The results indicate that ACTF-Net may improve situational awareness, resource usage, and response time in high-risk crisis situations.

With the rapid development of social media platforms, automated accounts have become an important factor affecting information dissemination, public opinion governance and platform ecology. This paper takes TwiBot-20 as the research object, focusing on the study of social bot detection based on textual semantic information and social topological information. The research objective of this paper is to combine detection performance with readable expert evidence for social bot detection through a data-driven dual-expert model. Firstly, a textual semantic expert based on supervised fine-tuning large language model is constructed. User description, follower count, following count, tweet count, verification status and active years are organized as user profile input, and the textual semantic expert outputs the semantic-side prediction label and evidence summary. Secondly, a topological structure expert based on relational graph convolutional network is built. The construction of this expert includes the construction of user nodes, the construction of Following and Followers relation edges, and the construction of node features by combining account attributes and textual semantic embeddings. Thirdly, a dual-expert fusion reasoning model based on large language model is constructed. The outputs of textual semantic expert and topological structure expert are organized as structured evidence, and user-specific decision weights computed by a model fitted on the development split are used to guide the large language model to generate the final detection result and explanation report. The proposed model achieves 82.76% accuracy and 84.14% bot F1 on TwiBot-20, improving on the stronger single expert by 2.20 and 1.54% points. Its accuracy matches stacking, while the calibrated ensemble achieves a slightly higher bot F1. The model also produces readable reports of expert disagreement and decision cues, illustrated through correct and incorrect arbitration cases.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming every dimension of the fashion industry—from creative ideation and pattern generation to supply chain optimization, trend forecasting, and personalized retail. Yet the higher education institutions charged with preparing tomorrow’s fashion professionals remain structurally, pedagogically, and conceptually unprepared for this transformation. This paper argues that the challenge is not simply one of adding AI tools to existing curricula; it is, more fundamentally, a question of literacy. Drawing on a critical integrative review of interdisciplinary scholarship across AI education, digital literacy theory, fashion pedagogy, and industry workforce analysis, this paper examines three interlocking questions: What is AI literacy, and how has its conceptualization evolved? What theoretical and conceptual frameworks currently govern AI literacy discourse, and how might they be adapted for the creative disciplines? And, critically, do fashion higher education students require a form of AI literacy that is fashion-specific—and if so, what form should it take? The paper proposes a novel conceptual framework, the Fashion AI Literacy Framework ( FALF ) and outlines concrete curricular pathways for implementation. The framework is presented as a conceptual proposition that requires empirical validation. The argument advanced here is both urgent and structural: generic AI literacy, however well-designed, may not fully equip fashion students to navigate the creative, ethical, commercial, and cultural terrain that defines their discipline. On the evidence reviewed here, a domain-specific approach is better understood as needed rather than optional.

https://github.com/Borealiscodes/Geometric-Hallucination-Taxonomy/tree/main A Geometric Taxonomy of Hallucinations in Structural AI Systems (v1.0) introduces the Geometric Hallucination Taxonomy (GHT), a five‑class operator‑based framework that explains hallucinations as geometric instabilities in latent‑space manifolds rather than semantic or probabilistic anomalies. The taxonomy characterizes hallucinations through curvature blowout, spectral cascade, holonomy drift, topological collapse, and nonlinear fusion‑field dynamics, each corresponding to a distinct failure mode detectable through formal geometric operators. The preprint reframes hallucinations as manifold‑level events arising from deformation, collapse, rotational drift, rank instability, and nonlinear blending in latent representations. Existing interpretability tools—embedding similarity, token plausibility, attention patterns, SGI, Γ—operate on vector geometry and cannot detect these manifold‑level instabilities. GHT fills this gap by providing operators that measure curvature, eigenvalue trajectories, parallel transport behavior, rank stability, and nonlinear fusion‑field behavior. The taxonomy is supported by a complete operator layer implemented in the accompanying repository. Curvature, spectral, holonomy, topology, and fusion‑field operators are implemented in /toolkit/, demonstrated in six pedagogical notebooks in /examples/, validated through a deterministic PyTest suite in /tests/, and formally defined in /math_spine/. The preprint also includes a Lean‑ready formalization scaffold for future mechanized proofs. This structure ensures that every conceptual component has a concrete implementation, a reproducible test, and a formal mathematical definition. By treating hallucinations as geometric phenomena rather than semantic deviations, GHT provides a structural foundation for interpretability, safety, and the design of future geometric AI architectures. It positions hallucinations within the broader framework of structural AI, where models are understood as dynamical geometric objects rather than probabilistic text generators. The taxonomy serves both as a research contribution and as a navigational map of the geometric‑AI system it documents. --- Relation to Prior Work This preprint serves as an independent, external interpretive supplement to the geometric‑operator framework introduced in: Marín, J. (2026). A geometric taxonomy of hallucinations in large language models. arXiv:2602.13224. It is not authored by, endorsed by, or affiliated with the authors of that work. Instead, it extends the geometric‑operator perspective by providing a structural taxonomy of hallucination modes grounded in curvature, spectral dynamics, holonomy, topology, and nonlinear fusion‑field operators. ---

(A) Background: This work provide a novel statement-level fault localization technique that combines Large Language Model (LLM) with statistical, evolution and test-coverage features on a five-stage pipeline. Notably, we employ five algorithms for performance comparison. We also investigate the propagation of faults from a framework to its downstream dependency applications (100 applications) in Machine Learning (ML) and non-ML domain across Java and Python programming language. We are motivated to carry out this study because of the ever-growing integration of LLM into modern software application so that quality of such application is kept up-to-date optimally from the angle of fault localization and fault propagation. Next, we evaluate our approach on existing baseline fault localization techniques on baseline datasets (Defects4J and Tests4Py) in which our result outperforms the best existing techniques on the baselines. Furthermore, we evaluate our approach with stand-alone Claude reasoning model on baseline datasets (Defects4J and Tests4Py) and we found that the Top-1 prediction of our approach outperforms Claude's Top-1 prediction. Hence, we justify our study applicability to real-world scenarios. We provide the step-wise approach of our implementation below. documents.abstract: Clinical biochemistry generates approximately 70% of the objective data used in medical decision-making, yet the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and large language models (LLMs) into laboratory operations remains fragmented. Existing digital-health maturity constructs (HIMSS EMRAM, HITI, CAMM) do not jointly address analytical metrology, algorithmic lifecycle governance, and clinical outcome accountability, leaving laboratories without a structured roadmap for AI-augmented diagnostic stewardship. To develop and face-validate the biochemistry–AI Stewardship Maturity (BASM) framework, a system-level maturity model that links laboratory analytics, AI governance, and health-service outcomes across five progressive tiers. A PRISMA-ScR-guided scoping review of six databases (MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Cochrane) covering January 2022–July 2026 identified 1,482 records; 29 sources were retained after dual-independent screening (Cohen’s κ = 0.86). Charted evidence was triangulated with IFCC, ADLM, CAP, and CLSI position statements, and consolidated into a seven-dimension rubric. Face validity was assessed with five laboratory directors, and structural comparisons were performed against four precedent maturity models. BASM operationalizes maturity across seven dimensions—analytical foundations, data infrastructure, algorithmic lifecycle governance, diagnostic stewardship, workforce competency, equity and safety, and outcome accountability—resolved into five ordinal tiers (BASM-1 to BASM-5) with 12–24-month transition milestones. A chain of custody aggregation rule prevents high analytical scores from masking governance or equity deficits. Alignment with TRIPOD + AI, DECIDE-AI, and TRIPOD-LLM reporting standards is embedded at tiers 3–5. BASM provides laboratories, health systems, and regulators with an actionable, standards-aligned instrument to plan, benchmark, and audit AI-augmented diagnostic stewardship. A multi-institutional modified-Delphi validation is the priority next step.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled clinical decision support systems (CDSSs) increasingly combine structured clinical data and medical images, but their explanations differ in cost, format, storage, and failure behavior. This study presents a modality-adaptive software architecture for a browser-based CDSS supporting 10-year coronary heart disease (CHD) prediction, 30-day hospital readmission prediction, and chest-radiograph classification with 14 independent output scores. The architecture treats explanation selection as a request-time service policy: Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) accompany tabular predictions; local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) are requested separately; gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) and its generalized variant (Grad-CAM++) are computed only for threshold-positive classes within the five highest-ranked scores; and large language model (LLM) narratives are attempted when configured. React, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and a seven-day Redis cache implement the design. Seven synthetic fixture families satisfied the specified selection conditions. In a backend experiment involving 7,818 radiographs, heatmap generation averaged 140.2 ms per radiograph, or 78.2% of the 179.3-ms mean total. A separate in-process service-layer test completed all 3,600 requests successfully using deterministic prediction and explanation substitutes and SQLite persistence. The architecture specifies bounded explanation work and separate retention paths. Full-stack performance, clinical-model calibration, explanation quality, and clinician benefit remain subjects for future evaluation.

documents.abstract: This article analyzes the effects of GAI- Generative Artificial Intelligence- on contemporary forms of perception, language, and symbolic connection. Based on an interdisciplinary approach—drawing from philosophy, semiotics, and sociology—the study explores the collapse of critical and sensitive perception amidst the informational saturation of digital media, particularly in the context of the so-called “dead internet.” Using Generation Z as a paradigmatic expression of a new cultural sensibility, the paper discusses the transformation of authorship regimes, the dissolution of the public sphere, and the blurred boundaries between human and machine in meaning-making processes. This research investigates inflection points between classical models of reason and emerging aesthetic experiences shaped by technology. In the midst of symbolic emptiness, the concept of re-enchantment of the world (Maffesoli) is presented as a potential response—restoring presence, shared language, and affective bonds. The analysis seeks to foster a critical reflection on the role of culture, ethics, and communication in mediating the impacts of artificial intelligence, and emphasizes the urgency of symbolic reconfiguration in an era of perceptual collapse.

Abstract. Wind and solar energy are two popular alternative energy sources. However, wind turbines are larger and more complex than solar panels. Accordingly, wind turbines are more exposed to environmental factors and therefore more prone to mechanical failures. Our work improves the reliability and efficiency of wind energy systems by presenting an artificial intelligence (AI)-based system that predicts mechanical gearbox and electrical failures. Historical data are aggregated with real-time sensor data to train the prediction model. Apart from related mechanical and environmental data, sensors provide real-time vibration, internal nacelle temperature, wind speed, noise and smoke levels. The developed system integrates AI and Large Language Model (LLM)-based interfaces for real-time interactive monitoring of turbines. The user interface of the developed system allows users to receive informative responses on performance, detected risks, predicted failures, and energy production levels. The developed model has been validated using 5-fold cross-validation based on Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and ROC-AUC. The model achieves approximately 89.68 % Accuracy, 90.08 % F1- Score, 95.65 % ROC-AUC, and novel metric 65.13 %, Overall Performance. The performance results demonstrate the promising potential of AI- and LLM-integrated systems for wind energy applications. Prototype data, labeled via the XGBoost model trained with SCADA data, was retrained using the LightGBM algorithm, achieving 98.37 % Accuracy, 99.16 % F1-Score, 98.95 % ROC-AUC and 94.65 % Overall Performance; the analysis proved that the newly added gas and sound sensors significantly improved the fault prediction performance of the system.

Abstract While Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable zero-shot learning capabilities, their deployment in real-time interactive systems is constrained by sparse terminal feedback in long-sequence generation, unstable policy updates, and the computational overhead associated with verbose outputs. To address these challenges, this paper formalizes autoregressive text generation as a discrete-time Markov decision process (MDP) and proposes a latency-aware composite reward optimization framework based on proximal policy optimization (PPO). The core contribution of the proposed method is a multidimensional sequence-level terminal reward that jointly evaluates semantic coherence, lexical diversity, and computational cost. Specifically, a Natural Language Inference (NLI) cross-encoder evaluates the semantic consistency between the input context and the complete generated response, while Shannon entropy and Distinct-N metrics encourage lexical diversity. In addition, a hardware-aware penalty based on generated sequence length and measured inference latency discourages unnecessarily verbose outputs and promotes computationally efficient generation. During policy optimization, the terminal composite reward is propagated through generalized advantage estimation, while a token-wise Kullback–Leibler divergence term regularizes the updated policy against the reference policy. This formulation does not introduce token-level semantic rewards; instead, it combines informative sequence-level evaluation with step-wise policy regularization to improve empirical training stability. We evaluated the proposed framework on a large-scale hybrid corpus containing approximately 320,000 dialogue turns, including real-world English interaction data. Compared with the standard PPO baseline, the proposed method exhibited faster empirical convergence and lower variability in the observed training trajectories. It achieved a BLEU-4 score of 22.87 and a Distinct-2 score of 21.59%, while reducing the average inference latency to 42.8 milliseconds per token under the reported hardware configuration. These results demonstrate the potential of latency-aware composite reward optimization to balance response quality, lexical diversity, and inference efficiency in real-time domain-specific LLM applications.

We formulate a common discrete configuration space in which edge lengths encode piecewise-flat geometry, a causal orientation defines a partial order, and compact gauge holonomies on the same oriented edges represent the local gauge group of the Standard Model. A single formal configuration sum combines a four-dimensional Regge gravitational action, Wilson-type gauge actions, a Higgs sector, and a chiral matter sector. We derive the local gauge-transformation laws and show that face-trace actions are gauge invariant. We state a conditional stability result for a finite Euclidean edge regulator and explain why it does not establish stability of the full Lorentzian gravitational path integral. On a regular-lattice regulator, the standard low-momentum lattice dispersion is recovered as a calculation within the regulator, not as a prediction of the irregular dynamical network. The Newtonian limit is recovered conditionally if the geometry sum has a continuum phase governed by the Einstein–Hilbert action. This construction is a synthesis/ansatz, not a demonstrated Theory of Everything: the measure over complexes, the chiral lattice fermion operator, renormalized continuum limit, and a derivation of the Standard Model parameters remain unresolved. The common carrier of interactions should not be confused with unification of their couplings or symmetries. Acknowledgements: The author expresses gratitude to family, peers, and independent researchers for technical feedback on the mathematical infrastructure. Computational synthesis, linguistic polishing, and manuscript structural formatting assistance were supported by large language model AI assistants (Gemini and ChatGPT).

Biobank-scale imaging-genomic cohorts enable genome-wide association studies (GWASs) of organ structure and function. Traditional approaches rely on expert-defined image-derived phenotypes (IDPs), which capture only a fraction of the biological variation in high-content images. Powered by artificial intelligence, self-supervised learning (SSL) learns representations directly from intrinsic image structures, creating scalable, data-driven traits. Here, we review the technical frameworks and challenges of SSL-based imaging genetics and their applications in brain MRI, cardiac MRI, and retinal imaging. Early studies suggest that these data-driven approaches can complement traditional IDPs and may expand the phenotypic space available for discovery of heritable imaging traits, although broader validation across cohorts, ancestries, scanners, and imaging protocols remains needed.

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used in software development for coding, debugging, documentation, and learning. This study examines its adoption, benefits, challenges, security concerns, dependence, learning support, and future impact. Survey responses from 21 programming students and professionals were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, and average ratings. Of the respondents, 95.2% reported daily or frequent use and 95.2% used ChatGPT. Debugging and error fixing was the most common task (71.4%). Respondents reported benefits such as better problem-solving and faster development, but also identified bugs, security issues, architectural complexity, and privacy concerns. Overall, GenAI is viewed as a useful assistant, but human review, testing, and responsible use remain essential. The findings are exploratory due to the small sample size.

Data storage and processing have been fundamentally changed with the advent of cloud computing, which offers options for accessing computing resources with a certain level of flexibility and depends on the scale. However, this convenience provides a lot of room for security vulnerabilities where attackers can compromise systems, exfiltrate personal information, and, in many cases, the most pressing security threats are posed by individuals who have access to the corporate infrastructure legitimately. To counteract such problems, enterprises use multi-layered security architecture. Rather than just using a password as authentication, modern systems require multi-factor authentication, which can be any combination of a password and a text message containing a one-time password, a biometric scan, or both. Once you have access, policies are in place concerning what you are allowed to do, and organizations will often assign specific, discrete roles like manager or employee to different types of users associated with certain levels of permission and access. Authorization models are often followed like role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC), which explicitly specify user privileges inside cloud environments. The world of cloud security has witnessed an exponential growth in recent years, as organizations are using increasingly more artificial intelligence (AI)-based solutions to identify anomalous behaviors that may indicate an imminent attack. The hegemonic “never trust, always verify” paradigm has taken root in the realm of the cloud, carefully checking every request before giving access or permission to the same, regardless of its origin. Implementing these safeguards is not only important to thwarting attacks but to meeting basic requirements in protecting sensitive information, preventing unauthorized modification, and ensuring continuity in the event of incidences, thus providing data privacy. Finally, organizations are legally and industry required to meet various standards for the protection of customer data, further making it a complex task to plan and implement effective cloud security strategies.

Fatal railway level crossing crashes represent a public safety challenge. Existing data on these crashes is limited, mostly focusing on frequencies rather than providing an in-depth understanding of the underlying causes. This study aimed to demonstrate the utility of using coronial findings, supplemented with reports from investigation agencies, to understand the system-wide factors contributing to railway crossing crashes and to explore the proposed recommendations. A systems thinking accident analysis approach, the AcciMap technique, underpinned the analysis. Over a 20-year period, 151 cases were identified, involving a range of road user types. Of these cases, 135 included sufficient detail to extract contributory factors and recommendations. A total of 483 contributory factors were extracted and used to develop an aggregate AcciMap. Most factors were associated with road user behaviour and/or individual characteristics, as opposed to systemic issues. Unique contributory factors were identified for crashes occurring at active crossings (those with dynamic warnings present) versus passive crossings (those with signage only). A total of 184 recommendations were extracted and mapped using the AcciMap framework. Recommendations tended to take a system-wide view of preventing future occurrences, acknowledging the complexity of managing risk at the interface of two transport modes. The analysis provided important information to support crash prevention efforts, including a set of common systemic recommendations identified from the data that require collaborative efforts across road and rail stakeholders. Mechanisms for supporting this collaboration should be further explored. The study also provided learnings regarding the nature of coronial investigations and areas for potential improvement.

Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurotype experienced among children and adolescents worldwide. Students with ADHD often face challenges with academic motivation and achievement which impacts their academic achievement at school. Factors contributing to these challenges include difficulty with sustaining attention, planning and organisation of tasks and activities, and time management. At school, students with ADHD experience challenges initiating learning tasks, particularly those of which they are not interested or are perceived to be overwhelming to start. Students with ADHD who lack motivation to start and engage in learning activities decrease their ability to remain on task resulting in disengagement from learning. Lower academic achievement in school is linked to poorer educational attainment (e.g., fewer years spent in compulsory schooling or post-secondary education) and occupational outcomes (e.g., lower income, higher unemployment) for individuals with ADHD post schooling. This systematic review explores the role of academic motivation on academic achievement among students with ADHD. The review identified a paucity of research with only three published papers (representing two independent samples), published between 2020 and 2023, meeting the inclusion criteria. Findings showed that both amotivation and cognitively challenging task motivation negatively predicted grade point average. Results also found that extrinsic and intrinsic motivation positively predicted academic outcomes. These findings indicate that supporting the academic achievement of students with ADHD is critically important for learning and academic success at school. These data also expand this important area of research beyond formal schooling to higher education and the workplace to ensure that students with ADHD continue to realise successful university and career outcomes. Additionally, future research could explore the role of extrinsic motivation as a strategy to support academic achievement among those with ADHD, or act as a stepping stone toward developing more intrinsically oriented forms of motivation.

Minority and underserved youth are less likely to undergo diabetic retinopathy screening, yet more likely to have diabetic retinopathy. We hypothesize that autonomous artificial intelligence-based diabetic eye exams could mitigate screening disparities in minority youth. This prospective study enrolled 397 White and non-White youth with type 1 (72%) and type 2 (28%) diabetes at diabetes care visits. Participants underwent autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exams and optical coherence tomography imaging. The primary outcome is equivalence in screening completion between White and non-White youth. The secondary outcome is diagnostic accuracy of AI against prognostic standard. At baseline, participants in the White cohort were more likely to have completed a prior diabetic eye exam (79.8% v 61.8%, p < 0.0001). Following the artificial-intelligence intervention, 99.5% in the White cohort and 98% in the non-White cohort completed the autonomous artificial-intelligence diabetic eye exam, demonstrating equivalent screening completion after implementation. When compared to standard grading, AI demonstrated sensitivity of 100% (95% CI: 67.6%, 100%), and specificity of 76% (95% CI: 71.4%, 79.9%) for detecting more than mild diabetic retinopathy. Implementation of autonomous AI at the point of care increases access to and completion of diabetic eye exams, achieving equivalent screening completion among White and non-White youth, suggesting the potential to reduce disparities in diabetic retinopathy screening. Study Registration: NCT05463289. This study demonstrates that autonomous AI screening for diabetic retinopathy can achieve equivalent screening completion among white and non-white youth with T1D, suggesting the potential to reduce disparities in diabetic retinopathy screening.

Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.

Abstract We develop an active inference route-planning method for autonomous control of an intelligent agent. The aim is to reconnoiter a geographical area while balancing search and tracking behaviors to maintain a dynamic situational awareness map. To achieve this, we construct an evidence map that reflects our current understanding of the situation, integrating both positive and “negative” sensor observations of possible target objects collected over time, and diffusing the evidence across the map as time progresses. The generative model of active inference uses Dempster-Shafer theory and a Gaussian sensor model to provide input to the agent. The generative process employs a Bayesian approach to update a posterior probability distribution. We calculate the variational free energy across all locations within the sensor radius by assessing the divergence between a pignistic probability distribution of the evidence map and a posterior probability distribution of the target object, including the level of surprisal associated with receiving new observations. Using the variational free energy, we direct the agent’s movement in simulation by taking incremental steps toward a position that minimizes the variational free energy. This approach addresses the challenge of balancing exploration and exploitation, allowing the agent to search large areas while efficiently tracking identified targets. Across 1000 simulation trials, the approach surpasses benchmarks in target observation by an average of 51%–69% across various metrics for a 100-meter sensor radius.

Autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents now plan, call tools, change records and delegate work to other agents at machine speed. Most enterprise controls assume a human decides and a deterministic application executes, so they do not cover this. The Agentic Defence and Assurance Model (ADAM) is a proposed operational framework for governing, securing and assuring AI agents in the enterprise. Its foundational proposition is that autonomy must never exceed accountability. ADAM has three architectural dimensions. Governance and Accountability sets the conditions under which agents may operate. Six Operational Security Layers (PREVENT, CONSTRAIN, DETECT, INTERRUPT, RECOVER and REVALIDATE) provide the runtime controls. Continuous Assurance and Evidence demonstrates that those controls work. Four capabilities cut across all six layers: agent identity, delegated authority, independent enforcement and operational telemetry. The report also introduces several proposed constructs: the Agent Autonomy Envelope, a four-tier agent risk classification, a catalogue of 29 controls, a six-point maturity scale with three separate assessment dimensions, and two exploratory metrics. ADAM is designed to complement NIST, ISO/IEC, OWASP and MITRE resources, not to replace them. Version 0.1 is published for comment. This record contains the technical report (PDF), the framework diagrams (PDF and editable SVG), the briefing presentation (PDF) and the control catalogue (CSV).

Abstract Graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as an effective framework for biological sequence classification using De Bruijn graphs, yet node representations have received comparatively less attention. Although multiscale Expected Density of Nucleotide (EDN) provides informative sequence-level representations, it cannot be directly incorporated into graph-based sequence learning because De Bruijn graphs require node-level representations. To address this challenge, we propose Contextual Multiscale Expected Density of Nucleotide (cMSEDN), a lightweight, deterministic framework that adapts multiscale EDN sequence representations into sequence-specific node embeddings for De Bruijn graph learning while preserving k-mer identity and incorporating occurrence-level context. Unlike static k-mer encodings, cMSEDN aggregates occurrence-level contextual features so that identical k-mers can receive distinct sequence-specific representations across different biological sequences. We evaluated the proposed framework on seven biological sequence classification datasets spanning transcription factor binding prediction, promoter recognition, and RNA subcellular localization across multiple species, and encompassing both DNA and RNA sequence analysis tasks using GCN and GIN architectures. Compared with conventional context-independent node representations, off-the-shelf foundation models serving as static node-feature extractors, and a static EDN-based baseline, cMSEDN consistently achieved improved classification performance across the benchmark suite for De Bruijn Graph Neural Networks while using compact deterministic embeddings. These results indicate that our sequence-specific k -mer encoding is an effective, computationally lightweight bio-sequence graph representation for sequence classification, requiring no modifications to the underlying GNN architecture.

This study examines the short-term educational contribution of teacher-guided generative tutoring through a secondary analysis of a randomized trial in nine public secondary schools in Benin City, Nigeria. Among 1328 randomized students, 657 were offered twelve 90 min sessions combining Microsoft Copilot, curriculum-aligned English activities, and pair work, while 671 received regular instruction. Intention-to-treat models used ordinary least squares, school fixed effects, baseline performance adjustment, and HC3 standard errors, with conditional estimates on observed endline outcomes and required covariates. The overall assessment effect was 0.310 SD (95% CI 0.176–0.444; n = 654), with positive estimates for English (0.238 SD), AI knowledge (0.309 SD), and school examination performance (0.206 SD). The digital-skills estimate was positive but imprecise (0.139 SD; p = 0.066). Attendance was positively associated with achievement, and effects were larger at higher baseline performance. The female interaction was positive, with caution warranted by the smaller male subsample. The digital-access interaction was negative but imprecise (−0.182 SD; 95% CI −0.370–0.005; 457 complete cases). These findings support short-term learning gains from the complete tutoring package relative to regular instruction. They provide a basis for further evaluation of structured programs integrating generative AI with curriculum, collaborative practice, and teacher guidance in resource-limited urban schools.

documents.abstract: Automation, artificial intelligence, connected sensing technologies, digital twins, robotics, and data-driven control systems are increasingly transforming textile and apparel production systems. However, in existing studies, these technologies have often been analyzed separately or limited to specific factories, countries, or specific stages of the production process. The study created an integrated analytical framework for analyzing the maturity of technology adoption in modern textile production systems, with a new dataset based on data collected from various sources related to technology adoption and digital readiness open to the public. The complete dataset contains a total of 8,198 analytical observations and 26 variables. The dataset covers nine manufacturing and business activities for the period 2019-2023 in five countries - Bangladesh, Chile, Ethiopia, India and Senegal. As part of this study, a subset of 5,472 production-based observations were used for predictive modeling. This subset is divided into 3,830 trainings, 821 validations, and 821 test observations, respectively, in a group-conscious manner. The study compared the performance of four models: Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine and One-Dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (1D CNN). The final results showed 92.00%, 93.00%, 93.56% and 96.10% accuracy respectively, making 1D CNN the highest performing model. In a test set of 821 observations, 1D CNN's class-based F1 score was 95.29% for Basic / Manual, 97.54% for Intermediate / Mechanized, 68.57% for Digital, and 95.20% for Advanced / Smart. In the supplied ROC analysis, the value of AUC was found to be 0.998094. Integrated Gradients-based Explainable AI analysis also indicates that country-specific context, clothing cutting and sewing activities, production-domain indicators, quality-management-related variables, survey duration, and internet access rate contribute significantly to model decisions. Overall, the results show that it is possible to effectively analyze the maturity of technology adoption by combining various publicly available technology indicators with machine learning and deep learning. At the same time, class inequalities and limitations in the comparability of data from different countries have also been identified, which are important considerations for future research and external verification.
